usage: Warm reassuring reply, like 'I get it, it's okay'
Note the 가-subject: comprehension fails on its own, no 를
Asking someone to be understanding of your situation
이해 as a noun with 빠르다, describing a quick mind
examples: Object + 를 when YOU actively grasp something
조금 softens it to 'a bit', very humble and natural
I totally understand how you feel
Casual 반말 to a close friend; 마음 = feelings, not 'mind'
nuance: 이해하다 is Sino-Korean: 理解 means 'untie/loosen (解) the logic (理)', so it pictures a tangled idea coming apart in your head — it covers both intellectual comprehension AND emotional sympathy ('I understand how you feel'). The dividing line versus 알다 is crucial: 알다 is to KNOW a fact ('I know his name', 이름을 알아요), while 이해하다 is to make sense of WHY or HOW something works. As a 하다-verb it conjugates regularly (이해해요, past 이해했어요). The big English-speaker pitfall is the particle in the negative: 'I don't understand' is almost always 이해가 안 돼요 (subject 가 + 되다, lit. 'understanding doesn't form'), not the literal 이해를 안 해요, which sounds like you're refusing to understand on purpose. Also resist translating 'understand my feelings' as 내 감정 — Koreans say 내 마음을 이해하다.

Translating 'I don't understand' literally as 이해를 안 해요. That implies willful refusal. The natural form is 이해가 안 돼요 with 가, treating understanding as something that fails to occur.
Saying 내 감정을 이해해 주세요 for 'understand my feelings'. The idiomatic collocation is 마음 (heart): 내 마음을 이해해 주세요.

usage: Asking someone to put their faith in you
Short, blunt denial of a claim
Pleading to be trusted; 주다 adds the favor nuance
Fixed idiom prefacing something hard to believe
examples: Casual 반말; warm encouragement before a challenge
nuance: 믿다 is a single native word that spans two English verbs at once: to BELIEVE a fact/claim (그 말을 믿어요 'I believe that') and to TRUST a person (친구를 믿어요 'I trust my friend') — context, not a different word, tells them apart. The closest relatives are 믿음 (the noun, 'faith/trust') and the compound 신뢰하다 (信賴, the formal 'to have confidence in', used in business or writing); 믿다 is the warm, everyday spoken choice. Crucially, 믿다 keeps its ㄷ in the stem (믿어요, 믿었어요) — it is NOT a ㄷ-irregular like 듣다→들어요, so it never becomes *밀어요. Watch the homophone trap: that wrong *밀어요 collides head-on with the real verb 밀다 'to push' (밀어요), so one careless slip doesn't just misconjugate — it accidentally says 'push' instead of 'believe'. English 'believe in (a god/religion)' transfers fine: 신을 믿어요, 종교를 믿어요.

usage: Warm closing line in a card or message
The key pattern: verb + 기를 바라요 to hope a whole event happens
바라다 + 는 게 to nominalize 'the thing I hope'
examples: I hope for a good result
Noun + 를; hoping for an outcome
Verb + 기를 바라다 = hope an action happens
I hope things go well for you
Casual; 잘되길 is 잘되기를 shortened in speech
nuance: 바라다 is to HOPE or WISH FOR something, especially good things for other people, which gives it a warmer, more selfless feel than 원하다 ('to want' for yourself). The sharp contrast learners need: 바라다 leans toward outcomes beyond your control that you wish would happen (평화를 바라요 'I hope for peace'), while 원하다 names a concrete desire you intend to get (돈을 원해요 'I want money'). Its signature grammar is verb-기를 바라다 ('I hope that ~ happens'): 합격하기를 바라요. THE famous pitfall: the present polite form is 바라요, but almost every Korean accidentally says/writes 바래요 — that 바래다 actually means 'to fade in color'! The textbook-correct form is 바라요 / past 바랐어요, even though 바래요 dominates casual texting. Don't confuse 바라다 (hope) with 바라보다 (to gaze at).

usage: 뭘 = 무엇을 shortened; direct but polite question
Noun + 를; stating a clear desire
As you wish / however you want
원하다 + 는 대로 = 'in the way one wants'
examples: Past tense; abstract noun as object
Please tell me what you want
원하는 걸 = 원하는 것을, 'the thing you want'
nuance: 원하다 is Sino-Korean (願 'wish/desire' + 하다) and means to WANT a thing or outcome — it takes a NOUN object (커피를 원해요 'I want coffee'). The critical contrast for English speakers is with -고 싶다: to want to DO an action, you cannot use 원하다, you must use the verb stem + 고 싶다 (가고 싶어요 'I want to go'), never 가는 것을 원해요, which sounds stiff and translated. Compared with 바라다 ('hope'), 원하다 is more direct, concrete, and self-centered — a desire you mean to fulfill, not a gentle wish. It also feels a touch more formal and forceful than 갖고 싶다 ('want to have'); a waiter or a contract uses 원하다. Pitfall: English 'I want to eat' tempts you to reach for 원하다, but the natural Korean is 먹고 싶어요. Reserve 원하다 for noun objects.

usage: Casual clipped form (하 dropped) to a friend
Subject 이 + 되다: worry arises by itself, no 를
Fixed collocation: 걱정을 끼쳐 드려서 죄송해요
examples: I worried a lot about the exam
많이 modifies the worrying; past tense
Don't worry, it'll all work out
Casual reassurance pairing the negative with 잘되다
nuance: 걱정하다 (걱정 = 'worry/anxiety' + 하다) is the everyday verb for being anxious or concerned about someone or something. Distinguish it sharply from 고민하다: 걱정하다 is feeling ANXIOUS about how things will turn out ('I'm worried about my grades'), whereas 고민하다 is actively DELIBERATING over a hard choice ('I'm agonizing over which job to take'). As a 하다-verb it splits in the negative — 걱정 안 해요 (separating the noun) or 걱정하지 않아요 — and the favor form 걱정해 주다 means 'to worry on someone's behalf', a kind gesture. The natural way to say 'I feel worried' is 걱정이 돼요 (걱정 + 이 + 되다), not 걱정을 해요, which sounds like deliberate worrying. The single most useful phrase in the whole language family is 걱정하지 마세요 ('don't worry') — memorize it. English 'I'm worried about you' is 네가 걱정돼 or 너를 걱정해, not 너에 대해 걱정해.

usage: 깜짝 is the mimetic adverb for a sudden jolt of shock
Calming phrase before delivering surprising news
It's nothing to be surprised about
놀랄 + 일 = 'a thing to be surprised at'
Causative: 깜짝 놀라게 해 줄게 'I'll surprise you'
examples: I was surprised to hear the news
-고 links the trigger (hearing) to the reaction
I was surprised by the price
Cause takes 에: 'surprised AT the price'
Hey, you scared me! I got startled
Casual; 놀랐잖아 nudges 'see, you made me jump'
nuance: 놀라다 is to BE SURPRISED, STARTLED, or SHOCKED — a sudden involuntary reaction, so it lives mostly in the past tense (놀랐어요 'I was surprised') because by the time you speak, the jolt already happened. Although it ends in 라, it is NOT a 르-irregular like 빠르다→빨라요; it conjugates straightforwardly: 놀라 + 았어요 → 놀랐어요. The cause of the surprise takes the particle 에 (가격에 놀랐어요 'surprised at the price') or the connector -고 (듣고 놀랐어요 'heard and was surprised'). Distinguish it from 놀다 'to play' — one extra ㄹ-syllable apart but utterly different. Its constant companion is the mimetic word 깜짝 ('with a start'): 깜짝 놀랐어요 is the default phrase. To say something IS surprising/amazing, switch to the adjective 놀랍다 (놀라워요). English speakers wrongly mark the cause with 를; remember the trigger gets 에, not the object particle.

usage: Object + 를; savoring a stretch of time
Note: for food Koreans say 맛있게 드세요, NOT 즐기세요
즐겨 + verb = 'habitually & with pleasure do': 즐겨 봐요
Common collocation, a YOLO-ish life motto
examples: Enjoy a NOUN directly; no extra verb needed
정말 intensifies; past tense after the event
nuance: 즐기다 means to ENJOY in the sense of actively savoring or relishing an activity — it is more deliberate and engaged than 좋아하다 ('to like'). The sharp distinction: 좋아하다 states a preference ('I like coffee', 커피를 좋아해요) and can apply to people you fancy, while 즐기다 means you actively partake in and take pleasure FROM something (커피를 즐겨요 'I enjoy/savor coffee', as a hobby or ritual). A very useful construction is 즐겨 + verb, meaning 'to habitually do X with pleasure': 즐겨 보다 ('enjoy watching, watch regularly'), 즐겨 듣다 ('enjoy listening to'). The biggest pitfall is English 'Enjoy your meal!' — do NOT say 식사를 즐기세요; the idiomatic phrase is 맛있게 드세요/잡수세요 ('eat deliciously'). Also note 즐기다 takes a noun object with 를, so 'enjoy reading' becomes 독서를 즐기다 or 책 읽는 걸 즐기다, not a bare verb.

usage: Firm, often defiant statement (noun split by 안)
Past action + 걸 후회하다 to regret a deed
후회막심 (後悔莫甚), an idiom for overwhelming regret
examples: Object + 를; the thing you regret
-아서 gives the reason for the regret
지금 안 하면 나중에 후회할 거야
If you don't do it now, you'll regret it later
nuance: 후회하다 is Sino-Korean — 後悔 literally stacks 後 'after' + 悔 'regret/remorse', i.e. the regret that comes AFTER the deed — and names the painful wish that you had chosen differently. It typically points backward (그 결정을 후회해요 'I regret that decision') and frequently pairs with a reason clause in -아서/어서 or with a past-action nominalizer -(으)ㄴ 걸: 그렇게 말한 걸 후회해. Distinguish it from 아쉽다, which is a milder 'it's a shame / I wish it were a bit different' about things often outside your control, whereas 후회하다 carries genuine self-reproach over your own past action. Also separate it from 미안하다 ('to be sorry' TO someone) — 후회하다 is regret felt inside, not an apology directed at another person. Pitfall: 'I regret to inform you' has no 후회하다 equivalent; that polite-letter formula becomes 안타깝게도 or 죄송하지만. Keep the object with 를, and remember the negative splits as 후회 안 해요.

usage: 혼자 = by oneself; the lonely, brooding nuance
What are you mulling over so hard?
고민 + 중 = 'in the middle of deliberating'
들어주다 = lend an ear to a worry
examples: I'm mulling over my career path
진로 (career direction) is a classic object of 고민하다
I deliberated for a long time
오래 = for a long while; past tense
I'm torn over whether to buy it or not
Casual; 살까 말까 = 'to buy or not', the agonizing-choice frame
nuance: 고민하다 is Sino-Korean: 苦悶 fuses 苦 'bitter/painful' + 悶 'anguish/stuffiness', so it literally paints a bitter, stuffy churning in the chest — it means to AGONIZE OVER or deeply DELIBERATE a hard problem or choice, heavier than plain 생각하다 ('to think'). The key contrast is with 걱정하다: 걱정하다 is anxious WORRY about an uncertain outcome, while 고민하다 is wrestling with a DECISION or a problem you're trying to solve (어느 대학에 갈지 고민해요 'I'm agonizing over which university to attend'). It also outweighs 생각하다, which is neutral thinking; 고민하다 implies the matter weighs on you. As a noun, 고민 means 'a worry/dilemma' (고민이 있어요 'I have something troubling me'), and 고민 중이에요 is the natural 'I'm still deciding'. Pitfall: don't use 고민하다 for light, pleasant pondering like daydreaming — that's just 생각하다. And it's a problem you mull, not a person.

Confusing 고민하다 (wrestling with a decision/problem) with 걱정하다 (anxious about an outcome). 'Worried about the result' = 결과를 걱정해요; 'agonizing over which to choose' = 뭘 고를지 고민해요.
Saying 고민이 해요. The noun pattern is 고민이 있어요 ('I have a worry') or 고민 중이에요 ('I'm deliberating'); the verb is 고민해요.

usage: 조금만 = just a bit; encouragement to bear with it
못 + 참다 = unable to endure; the breaking point
참을성 = patience (the noun derived from 참다)
Classic collocation with 눈물; also 웃음을 참다 'stifle a laugh'
examples: 화를 참다 = suppress anger, a very common pairing
I have to endure the pain
아픈 걸 = 아픈 것을, 'the painful thing'
I couldn't hold back my laughter
Casual past; 웃음 = laughter, with the cannot form
nuance: 참다 is a native verb meaning to ENDURE, BEAR, or HOLD BACK — both physical discomfort (아픔을 참다 'endure pain') and inner urges you suppress (화를 참다 'hold back anger', 눈물을 참다 'hold back tears', 웃음을 참다 'stifle a laugh'). The stem ends in ㅁ, so it is a REGULAR verb: add 아 → 참아요, past 참았어요 — never 참어요 (the bright ㅏ vowel governs the ending). Contrast it with 견디다, which is to withstand a prolonged hardship or pressure over time (고통을 견디다 'endure suffering', 더위를 견디다 'bear the heat'); 참다 leans toward actively restraining a momentary impulse, while 견디다 leans toward holding up under sustained strain. 참다 carries cultural weight — patience and self-restraint (참을성) are prized virtues. Pitfall: choose 참아요 not 참어요, and for an ongoing battle against hardship 견디다 often fits better than 참다.

usage: Direct question; the person showing anger is the subject
Don't take it out on me
한테 marks the target of the anger; casual
버럭 is the mimetic adverb for a sudden outburst
examples: Please don't get angry at me
한테 = at/to me; the recipient of the anger
He gets angry over small things
작은 일에 = at small matters; 에 marks the trigger
nuance: 화내다 literally combines 화 (火, Sino-Korean 'fire' = anger) + 내다 ('to put out, let out'), so it pictures LETTING THE FIRE OUT — to OUTWARDLY SHOW or express anger (raising your voice, scolding). The essential contrast is with 화나다 (화 + 나다 'to arise'): 화나다 is the anger RISING inside you, an involuntary feeling ('I'm angry / I got mad', 화났어요), while 화내다 is the active VENTING of it toward someone ('he got angry at me', 나한테 화냈어요). So 화났어요 = 'I feel angry' (inner state), but 화냈어요 = 'I lashed out' (outward act). The target of 화내다 takes 한테/에게 (나한테 화내다), and the trigger takes 에 (작은 일에 화내다). Pitfall: English 'I'm angry' is the feeling — use 화났어요, NOT 화냈어요, which would mean you displayed anger at someone. Keep 내다 (let out) and 나다 (arise) straight; one letter flips agent vs experiencer.

usage: Reassuring phrase to someone in fear
Object of fear + 를; describing another's fear
examples: The child is afraid of the dark
Object + 를; the child fears the dark
높은 곳 = high places; past tense
Snakes? I'm seriously scared of those
nuance: 무서워하다 is the VERB form built from the adjective 무섭다 ('scary/frightening') plus -어하다, the suffix that turns a feeling-adjective into 'to show/display that feeling'. This is the heart of the matter for English speakers: 무섭다 describes the OBJECT — 'X is scary' (개가 무서워요 'dogs are scary TO ME', expressing the speaker's own fear) — whereas 무서워하다 describes a PERSON outwardly being afraid of something and takes a 를-object: 개를 무서워해요 ('he is afraid of dogs'). Korean grammar reserves bare adjectives like 무섭다 mainly for the speaker's own felt state, so to report a THIRD person's fear you must use 무서워하다 (동생이 개를 무서워해요), not 동생이 개가 무서워요. The same -어하다 pattern drives 좋아하다 (from 좋다), 싫어하다 (from 싫다), 예뻐하다 (from 예쁘다). Pitfall: don't put 를 on 무섭다 (개를 무서워요 is wrong) — 무섭다 takes 가 for the scary thing; only 무서워하다 takes 를.
